thread_title: S. purpurea ssp. venosa Columbus Co, NC
breadcrumb: S. purpurea ssp. venosa Columbus Co, NC

posts.body_html:
The population of S. purpurea venosa from Old Dock, Columbus Co, NC is in full bloom (April 2013)! Every year, the plants get bigger and older, which means more flowers. Last year, maybe 5 or 6 of these plants bloomed, but now almost every single plant has a flower on it. It has taken many years to get them to this stage.

Flower sizes differ, and a few plants have petals that are lighter than others, but for the most part, the flowers are relatively the same. They are very fragrant during the day, especially when it is warm, but the fragrance goes away during the night. The individuals from this population are quite genetically diverse, and there's a huge range of trap shapes and sizes.

posts.body_html:
some new photos, taken 7/21/13 After these plants bloomed, it took a while before they formed clusters of new pitchers. The old pitchers from last year (fall 2012) lasted until about mid June. If you leave the old pitchers on for too long, they compete with the new pitchers for space and light, so it's important to get rid of them.

All of the pitchers shown below were produced in 2013-all of the old ones were taken off-look at how fat this plant is:




Some amazing veins and colors in this population:





A crappy night shot, but this gives you a good idea of what they look like overall. They tend to be the "fattest" around fall, so they still have more "filling in" to do:

I pretty much lost this entire population in 2014 when I moved, but I had them backed up in seed form. The seeds were 11 years old, and out of hundreds, maybe 10 of them germinated, but I got a few going now!

posts.body_html:
Good to hear not all was lost! Your previous post was looking awesome with all the high contrast veins.

I'm interested in hearing how you store seeds long term. That sounds like an important way to ensure population genetics stick around when clones haven't been distributed yet.
posts.body_text:
Good to hear not all was lost! Your previous post was looking awesome with all the high contrast veins.
I'm interested in hearing how you store seeds long term. That sounds like an important way to ensure population genetics stick around when clones haven't been distributed yet.

posts.body_html: I just put them in ziplock bags and place them in the refrigerator!  Thing is, with power outs, fluctuation in humidity with rain during the winter and moving the seeds, they get exposed to the elements and their shelf life is decreased. Even some packets that are stored in the same bag had zero viability, whereas others had at least some seeds sprout after many years.  no clue why some last longer than others when harvested, dried, and stored under identical conditions.
